source.title: Nonlinear processing with linear optics
source.authors: Mustafa Yildirim; Niyazi Ulaş Dinç; Ilker Oguz; D. Psaltis; C. Moser

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling in an optical image-classification model and reports both power-law-like loss trends and departures at high parameter counts attributed to saturation and overfitting.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own nPOLO scaling results on Imagenette and Fashion MNIST. Its citations to language-model scaling laws are not results from this study. Fig. 5 values are not given numerically in the supplied text; rows record only the authors’ explicit descriptions of the plotted outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own scaling sweep over layer width and depth on a new kind of system, simulated optical (nPOLO) image classifiers on Imagenette and Fashion MNIST. It reports test loss against parameter count (Fig. 5b, 5d) and calls the trend a power law similar to digital networks. That is a new-setting result on V5, plus a depth-at-fixed-parameter observation bearing on V4. It is not a challenge paper (T5), and it does not study language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that nPOLO shows power-law loss scaling akin to the OpenAI studies. They say deeper models beyond 4 layers gave no substantial gain because of overfitting and the dataset bottleneck, and that optimal performance needs balanced width and depth. They also say pursuing depth alone offers diminishing returns without more data and compute.
record.recipe_differences: This is an optical image-classification scaling study, not a language-model pretraining sweep over parameters, tokens and compute or a compute-optimal allocation study.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset limits and overfitting affect the high-parameter results; depth changes the onset of saturation.

fits_no_version.finding: Test classification accuracy rises with parameter count and then saturates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In optical nPOLO image classifiers, test accuracy increases with parameter count before saturating at a fixed dataset size.

record.code_released: All relevant code is available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
record.problems: The supplied text provides no numerical values or fitted exponents for Fig. 5, and reports no uncertainty for the scaling results. The authors attribute high-parameter deviations to overfitting and dataset limits; exact deviation and saturation thresholds are not stated.
record.rows_left_out: None. Cited results from other studies were excluded; Fig. 5 outcomes are represented only by the aggregate descriptions stated in the text because the supplied text gives no plotted values.

untested.parts: No language models; no data or compute sweeps.

Only depth is varied at a fixed parameter count. Width/depth aspect ratio and other architecture details are not varied, there are no language models, and no loss values are given for the shape comparison.
No exponent or fit is reported. Only parameter count is varied (dataset size fixed, compute not swept). Repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer and other modalities are not tested.
No exponents, fitting methods or parameter-counting choices are compared.

missing.what: Authors' statement that optimal performance relies on balanced scaling of width and depth; no row records it.
Data augmentation (random flip and rotation) was added during scale-up to reduce overfitting. This is a setup change across the sweep that affects the high-count points.

record.verdict_notes: All scaling evidence is the authors' prose about Fig. 5; the text gives no numbers, exponents or fit quality. The system is a simulated optical classifier with a linear digital readout. Its link to V4 is by analogy, since V4 was established for language models. The parameter range is roughly 2e3 to 8e6 (2NW^2), about three orders of magnitude. The record's T5 tranche is changed to T3, and the V7 labels are dropped.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests optical image-classification models, not language-model held-out pretraining loss or variation in parameters, tokens and compute.
No small-run fit is reported as predicting the loss of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep of parameter and token allocation is reported.
Architecture comparisons are limited to nPOLO depth configurations and the reported parameter-count range; the study does not establish the claim for other architectures.
Tests optical image-classification models, not other modalities or the listed repeated-data, fine-tuning and transfer regimes generally.
The classification tasks are trained as the study’s primary tasks, not reported as downstream tasks following pretraining.

Reports high-parameter deviations associated with overfitting and dataset limits, but does not estimate or compare fitted exponents, fitting methods, parameter-count conventions, training schedules, or compute-optimal splits.
